The expedition consisted ot the steamer Mississippi, (fl >g ship) frigate Itariian, sloop of war Albany, ship John Adams, Germantown, Decatur. Spitfire, Vixen, Scourge, Vesuvius, Hecla, Etna, Donita. Petrel and Iteefer. Among the vessels were distributed 150 men helonging to the Potomac, and 340 to the Ohio, both of which remained at this place. After some delay at the island of Lobos, awaiting the arrival of the sailing vessels, arid subsequently at sea, owing to a dispersion of t he vessels by a norther, every tiling was ready for landing on the morning of the 18th ins!., at which time the Missis sippi was anchored off the bar of I uspan river, while the other steamers, having had their masts taken out. and otherwise lightened in every possible wav, look in tow the gunboats and barges of the expedition, carrying in all about 1200 men, and two pieces of field artillery. The other vessels of the squadron remained at anchor tinder Tuspen shoals, which lie six or eight miles to the easiward of ibe bar. In crossing the bar the Spitfire led the way. and was followed by the Vixen aud the Scourge, each having a gun-boat in tow Two of the learners struck on the bar, but were not suflered to be stopped lot u moment.

They literally ploughed their way over it. By twelve o'clock the whole expedition succeeded in gaining an entrance of the river, notwithstanding the serious difficulties pieseated bv the breakeis ol the bar. Shortly afterward, every thing being in readiness for an attack, Com Perry hoisted bis broad pennant on board the Spitfire, and led the rest of the vessels up the river. After ascending it a! out five miles, two forts w 're discovered on the right bank, both of which opened upon the squadron. Immediately all the boats were manned with storming parties, and while the steamers arid gunboats were returning the fiie ot the torts they the boats dashed on ai d took poss> s. sion of the forts, the Mexicans ret rea 1 1 1 g down one side of the hill as the sailors ascended the other. The whole expedition now moved on steadily toward the town of Tnspan, but in a little while another fort, situated on a high hill, commanding the whole city, opened upon the vessels and bulges. At the same time volleys of musketry were fired by the enemy from the chapparal ; this latter fort w as also promptly attacked, and like the other two, was carried without the enemy waiting to cross bayonets, our noble tars proving themselves first rate fellows (or this species of hoarding work Simultaneously with the occupation of this fort, a division ol the expedition landed in the town, and took possession of it. The greater part of the inhabitants had fled and left but a lew scattering soldiers within reach ol our

balls. In the course of the contest seventeen men and officers were killed and wounded, ( apt. Talunll received a ball in the right elbow joint; Lieut. Jas. L. Parker, aid to the commodore, a severe wound in the upper part ot the left breast ; Lieut Whittle, a ties ft wound in "lie right leg, nr.d Lieut Harstein, a flesh wound in the right wrist and thigh. All the wounded, however, are doing well. Several gnus of the Tiuxton were found mounted upon the torts, all of which were recovered and brought on board the squadron Other articles belonging to the liuxton were likewise recovered. After retaining possession of the town from the 18ih to the ggd inst, the force was withdrawn and embuiked, leaving, however, the Albany, and gunboat Dei: for, under Captain Drcese, to guard and command the place. All the forts of the place were destroyed by our forces. There lining no farther work on the coast for the squadron. Com. Perrv, contemplated, we learn, a movement tow rd the interior, with a fine body of 2500 tars, thoioughly organized, should such a step be deemed advisable.

Anecdote of Aciiii.i.e Murat. þÿ The following curious anecdote made its first appearance in an English lonn, in this country, in the columns ol the New York Mirror. It was Uuusluted from the Courrier des Et its Unis. We may mention the name of a prince as having been, lor a time at leas', connected with the N. Orleans bar, M. AchilleMurat, son of the ex-king of Naples, who made his debut as an advocate there, and showed himsell a remarkable man, if not an orator. With a singularity, however, belonging to Ins character, he never appeared at the har a second time, and has since quilted the town and the country. We may, however, mention an anecdote of his stay here, winch rests on the authority of Ins mother, the i'rincess ol Lipoua. While Italy was a province of the empire, a mutiny broke out in t he garrison of Leghorn, ol so fuiious a character, as to exoile in a high degree, Napoleon's indignation. He was no friend ol insubordination, and resolved to crush it in the hud. and make a terrible example of the culprits. Achille Mural was charged with this painful duty, and set oil' for Leghorn without delay. When he arrived there, the insurrection had spent itself, and shame and remorse succeeded a temporary forgelfulness. However, the Emperot's orders were strict, lhat punishment be indicted. Murat called the soldieis together, and after reproaching them billet ly for their offence, required that the ringleaders of the mutiny should be given up, otherwise ten men out of the battalion would be drawn by

lot, and shot. The soldiers hung their heads, ' and professed themselves ready for any punishment the Linperor might inflict upon them, but begged the General not to foice them to turn informers against their comrades. Murat could not yield, and the ten whose names were drawn, were about to be carried oil, when three soldiers stepped to the front, and avowed themselves the instigators of the revolt. There was so much shame and contrition expiessed by the vieux moustaches , lhat Mural was deeply moved, lie stood silent awhile, then ordered the three criminals to be taken to prison, to be shot lite next morning. That same night, when every thing was quiet except I he measured step of the patrol, and the cry of sentinels on the walls, Murat was seated in his apartment, while before him stood thiee grizzled veterans, cap in hand, weeping like children. It was not death the heroes of Areola and Marengo feared þÿ it was to be disgraced þÿ to die the death of traitors ; thev wept, not for their lute but lot their ci lines!

" Listen 1" said Murat. "1 believe tnu are sorry for what you have done, and 1 want to save your lives To morrow, at day break, you will be led out to execution, outsid'e the city. 1 will take cure there shall be no spectators. The platoon will fire on you with blank cartridges, and you must fail down and remain motionless, till they match off the ground. A trusty man will be ready to put you into a close carriage ; a vessel sails to morrow for America, on board of which you will embutk. Here is a purse of gold for each of you. Will you promise to behave yourselves?" Everything happened as he had arranged it, and Napoleon thanked Murat for having taken the lives of only three of his soldiers þÿ The circumstance remained a secret until 1830, when Frince Achille Moral, walking in tiie suburbs of New Orleans, was caught in a shower. Ho sought shelter in the nearest house, n small arid plain one; a man arid wife, with their children, were the only inhabitants The inari had an austere, yet goodnatured face, and that stilfish walk which an old soldier can never get rid of. The prince remarked that t lie host eyed him fixedly, and seemed strangely agitated. The prince, on the other hand, sitting by the humble hearth, cast iiis eyes around (tie room with die idle curiosity of a man who has nothing to do. þÿ He rose, for he saw on the walls some coarse engravings of Napoleon's Generals and battleg. Above tliern were placed, under a laurel crown, two portraits of Mural, as genera! and as king.

"Have you ever served France ?" asked the prince. " Yes, sir," answered the host, not without some embarrassment " Where? þÿ and under whom ?" ' In Italy, under General Mural." The son of the soldier king field out his hand to his father's old comrade. " Your name, my brave fellow ?" " Claude Gerard ; might 1 ask, sir, þÿ " " I am Achille Murat." " h is true, then, and my eyes did not deceive me! You are the son of my General, of my King, and mv saviour I If I am now alive, if 1 have a wife and children, I owe it to him alone;" and thereupon the old soldier told the story we have sketched down, ofien interrupting it with blessings and exclamations of gratitude. The prince, whose singular character and aversion to society, led him to avoid the city, and wander about in the country, never, while fie remained in America, found any roof more welcome and visited none oftener, than that which covered the poor and humble abode of his father's companion in arms.

O Connell, must prove interesting to the generality of your readers, and I theietore, as an English physician called in to attend him, take leave to lay before you the lollowing statement " Do Monday, May 10, I saw .Mr O'Gon noli for the liist tone, and lie was then sutlering from piofusc and involuntary diarrhcee, with great pain of the abdomen under pressuic, stiong rapid pulse, 11 i lied face, &c. Mr O'Oonnell had also chrciiic. bronchitis of some vears' standing. From lite remedies employed these symptoms were much ameliorated, and on the morrow he scented con valcscent. But from Mr. O'CornieH's great repugnance t" swallow even the most simple medicine, this slate of improvement could not be followed up On the evening of I uesday (11th) the new symptom of congestion of the brain piesenlcd itself. Active measures were immediately had recourse to, and from them there was a decided improvement. Again the aid ol interi al remedies was denied, Mr. O'Gnunell refusing to lake any medi cine. Towards the evening of Wednesday (12th) the symptom increased. Mr. O'Conmil was restless, and sometimes slightly ineohient. Our former measure were again employed, but with slight success During Thursday all the symptoms increased with great tendency to sleep, from which however, he could easily be aroused ; the breathrug was much embarrassed ; circulation be-

- came difficult, and in some degree it distinct, and the mind wavered. Thmsday night was passed in a state of profound heavy sleep; with increased difficulty of breathing, and in addressing those about him, he imagined himsel! in London, and spoke to them as if there. On Friday lie was much worse, the breathing very laborious, the voice scarcely audible, and the words half formed; all iho symptoms had increased. In this state he lingered on till Saturday night, seemingly conscious of the presence of those about him, but neither attempting to move nor þÿspeak. My treatment of Mr. O't ounell was always in conjunction with Dr Beretta, of this place, and a young French physician, who had t.c» companied him trom Lyons, and, on the day preceding his demise, we had the advantage of consulting with Dr. Viviani, the oldest practitioner of Genoa, and of high þÿrepute. By Ins advice, and as a last resource, a farther application ol leeches to the temples was advised, but all was in vain ; he exptied last night at half past nine o'clock, p m., apparently suffering little pain. During the whole period of our attendance upon Mr O'Connell it was with the greatest difficulty he could he induced to take medicine or even necessary food, and he perseveringly abstained from drink fnr fully forty hours Had this been otherwise, the period of death might have been precrasiinnied, but his failing health and spirits, with constant tendency to cerebral congestion, rendered certain his death at no very distant period."

From the London Times, May 10 We have seldom had occasion to record an operation of war more revolting to every feeling of humanity and justice than the bombardment and capture of the city and castle of Vera Gruz by the American forces. In itself, indeed, the conquest af the strongest fortified position on the Mexican coast is the most important exploit of the campaign, and probably tbe most considerable enterprise ever attempted by the troops of the United States. But when we call to mind the unginated, and the purposes principled aggression in which which for the wur ori- it has been carried on, the more signal these achievements are, the more sinister is the light they cast on the policy of the American government. The lustre of the arms of the United States is tarnished by the infamy ot such a contest against an unollending and important enemy; and the horrors ot war, which can only be atoned for by a noble cause and an heroic bravery, have in this instance been aggravated by the detestable policy which sent forth the invading army, and by the miserable weakness of those against whom its prowess was þÿdirected. The American despatches relate, with an air of unconscious simplicity, one of the most atrocious and barbarous acts committed in modern times by the forces of a civilized nation. The mode adopted by Gen. Scott in conducting the siege was characteristic of the fierce and destructive spirit of a volunteer

and unpractised army. No attempt is made lo disguise the fact that the means taken by that officer to force the citadel of San Juan rie Ulua to surrender was the destruction of the city of Vera Cruz. Nearly 7,000 projecl.les were thrown into this devoted town duiing ihe three days and a half that the bombardment lasted, tine half of the buildings are said to be destroyed. In fact, the attack appears to have been exclusively directed on ihe city, in preference to the castle, for General Scott expressly states, that the heavy pieces of ordnance on which he relied for Ihe reduction of the principal forts were not landed when the city was invesied ; and that he was surprised to find that the capitulation of the town and of the citadel was simultaneous. The tiling itself is so exiraordioarv, and so contrary lo all the usages of modern war, unless under circumstanscs of peculiar necessity, that we could not have believed it on any lower authority than that of the officer in command. As for the Castle of St. Juan de Ulna, it is one of those places into which a hostile force would find it difficult to make its way, if there were not a garrison to open the gates of it, and governor to sign a capitulation. It evidently surrendered to mere intimidation or corruption. or possibly to the desire of saving the city from total annihilation. The application of the foreign Consuls on the 24th of Match for a truce to enable themselves and tbe subjects of the European powers, together wt'A

Mexican women and children, to Jeave the city, was refuted by (Jenerul Scutt. Probably when those gentlemen resolved to teens: at their posts at tbe comn>eneetitent oi tf«a siege, they did tJOt anticipate that tie dilf

Was lo be the principal mark of the American fcftttenes or they might liuve consulted their own safety by retiring to those strong fortifications of the Castle, against which tfie enemy's artillery was riot directed, or on which, et least, it made no serious impression. The whole operation lasted twentv djtvs from the disembarkation of the troops, on the 9th of March, to tlte evacuation of the city and castle by the Mexicans on the 29lh. The rtogonation for a surrender began on the 26ih. þÿ During the It! days of active hostilities there were five dnvs of violent northers," those effectually interrupt hurricanes oH the coast of Mexico which all communion; - s hv sea, and must have placed tfie squadron :n considerable peril. For two <i:i\ s and w_ vs the wind was so violent, and the drifting sand so damaging, that it was almost impossit'Je to clear the trenches or to man the batteries. Yet, in spite of all these untoward circumstances, we ate informed that in the course of the whole series of operations, including the landing of 13,000 men and the storm of shot and shell from the woiks of die town and of San Juan de Ulna. the combined forces of the United States lost but 17 men killed, or in all 65 killed and wounded On the side of the .Mexicans t he loss of life and property is reported to have been frightful ; and that unhappy country seems to lie a prey to the accumulated horrors of anarchy and war, of cowardice and corruption, of foreign violence and domestic, pillage. In the city of
Mexico itself all order and law arc at an end. The government is extinct; the army defeated and dissolved.

If a nation could suddenly expire: this would be the supreme hour of the Mexican people ; us it is, the horrors inflicted on the aboriginal inhabitants of the country by their Spanish conquerors have been faithfully revenged upon the abject descendants of thoso conquerors by a race of men animated by equal passions and armed with equal superiority. The standard of the Spanish race in Mexico has been trampled on as bruta'ly and fiercely as t he ensigns of tfie tr.gennous and unfortunate people which preceded them in the occupation of that magnificent region. The compassion which these calamities naturally excite in our minds is, indeed, considerably mitigated by tfie irresistible contempt the world must entertain for a people which has shown itself to he so, thoroughly incapable of the first duties of existence of government, arid of self defence. On froth sides, the spectacle we have before our eyes is the opprobrium of the age we live in, and an indelible disgrace to the people of the New World, who professed to have planted their institutions on a higher basis than the lust of bloodshed and aggrandizement which have so often devastated the elder continent The sanguinary spoliation which incites the armies of t he United Stales is as degrading to mankind as the pnltionnery of their victims, for we cannot call them antagonists ; and whilst we should blush to applaud the military It iuniphs of the United Suites, wo can hardlv deign to pity the woful discomfiture of mi emasculated people.

It is, however, as ceituin as the lessons of history and lite justice of I'rovidrnce ean make it. that these great nets of political wrong lead straight to their own chastisement mild that everv hour of success in this fatal war will tie expiated hv years of trouble and embai rassment lu itic aggressors. From the St. Thomas Times, July 17, 1817. SPAIN. The Madrid mail of the 2nd instant lias brought us the papers of thal date, together with a mass of corn spondence from Spain. A considerable controversv continues to be carried on by the journals about the devotee question, and the succession to the throne in the event of i he Queen thing without issue ; hut there are certain organs of tire press which protest against the assumption that there is any truth in the statement of the Progressist party, that the Moderado party is desirous of keeping up a devision between the Quern. and her consort, or of interfering with the Queen's prerogatives, in order to pave iho way for the Dutchess do Montpeiisier being brought forward. As icg.ard the King, however, it would appear that he persist in lemai .ing at the Pardo, but the journal ate silent as to Ins movements. It appears that the Queen Christina has written to the Queen to request permission i

3 t t> j a: A 'T Jt 3« to return to Spain, anil some accounts sav Unit the Queen said she had no objection if the Ministers had none; while others say thal she only sent for answer, that the matter concerned her Ministers, not iter. From what we learn from our letters, there does not appear to be any intention on the part of the Queen-Mother to return to Madrid, at least for the present. It is saitl that Forcadell is to become the Chiet ol the Montemolenist partisans in Catalonia, the post being vacant by the death of Tristany and Kos de Ernies. He is said to be an able and popular man. liv a decree ol the Queen of Spain, issued, on the 2d, inst., the Prince of Peace is authorised to return into Spain, and resume all his ti les and honours. A Commission is appointed to settle the indemnities to be awarded to him. The Tiempo which is believed to have access to correct information, stales that Genetnl Espurtcro is included in the amnesty which is about lo be published, but that he will not be allowed to reside in Madrid for the present. Permission lias just been given to Generals I rime and Levmerie, and to Seuor liamon line to return from exile. The Clamor Publico says that incendiary proclamations against the Queen have been profusely distributed in the army and provinces. The HeralJo says that it has received a confirmation of the statement of the Spanish troops having entered Valenza do Mino in Portugal, after having driven away the insurgents. It adds that they have garrisoned it in conjunction with the troops of the Queen

ol Portugal, and intended to make it the base of future operations. Disturbances took place at Granada on the 28th ult., on account of the excessive dearness of food. Women were the ringleaders of the mob, whose cry was þÿ Bread at eight cuartos ! We are hungry! We want bread þÿI The soldiers and authorities were insulted, hut at last the people were dispersed before they could commit any very serious acts of violence. At Gijon on the 29tlt, the lower classes rose to prevent the embarkation of corn, and then proceeded to act in a violent manner. They treated with contempt the remonstrances of the authorities; and when the troops were called out they attacked them. Orders were given to the soldiers to fire, and many ol the rioters were killed or wounded. This exasperated the mob, who rushed on the soldiers and completely defeated them. The corn was then pillaged, and several houses were broken open. From the New York Express, June 18. ITALY. and good Pope is already beginning to he imitated by tin ptinee of Italy. The Giaud

From the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin, June 9, 1847. THE LONDON TIMES. The London Times, in noticing the fall of Vera Cruz, speaks of the siege as þÿ one of the most atrocious and barbarous acts committed in modern times by the forces of a civilized þÿnation. As thal orthodox journal never jokes, we must suppose it means what it says. Our own memory, however, is more tenacious than that of the Times, and we will therefore recall to mind a few sieges which, in our humble opinion, at least rival that of Vera Cruz in atrocity. But before we do this, let ns say a word on the manner in which the fall of Vera Cruz is spoken of in France, and even among the more liberal presses of England. The opinion of one of these latter we gave the other day ; and it here testimony, though unwillingly, to the gallantry of our troops. It is in Fiance, however, that this siege has received the highest applause, where it has been of signal service lo us, by raising the estimate of our prowess, resources and energies. France is essentially a military country, and can appreciate military deeds better than any nation in Europe; and in France respect for the United States, and a conviction of the policy of conciliating us, is daily gaining ground. In spite of their antipathies to republicanism, Louis Phillippe and his Cabinet are forced to acknowledge ilint America has risen to be a first rate military power, as she has long been a first tale commercial one. Two sieges are memorable in the history of this century, Copenhagen and Badnjoz ;

and in both, Great Britain played a prominent part. The origin of the first is a curious, but instructive study. It was dutiug the height of the struggle between England and Napoleon, that the former began to suspect the amicable feelings ol Derunaik towards herself. Now Denmark was an independent nation, and had a rigid lo choose either side in the controversy, nor was she liable, aecording to the law of nations, to he treated as an enemy until she committed some overnet of hostility against Great Britain. But Denmark possessed a fleet not very large it is true, yet sufficiently numerous to render its falling into þÿNapoleon hands s bv no means desirable for England ; and accordingly, w ithout a moment s hesitation, and in dr lianee of the acknowledged tight of neutrals, the latter power sent a naval force to Co peril- agen, demanding the surrender of the Danish fleet. This high handed and insolent de. wand the Danish Crown þÿ1 rin.ee had tin spirit fo refuse. Thcu ensued a scene which was

truly « one of the most atrocious ami bar- j bn þÿroux of modern times. For hours the fcnglish fleet hailed lire and hall on the demoted town, and on the hastily constructed batteries where the heroic Danes made a desperate struggle for their nationality. Hut their Courage and devotion were in vain. þÿ Tire British triumphed, in consequence of their overwhelming numbers The Danish Beet was seized A more flagrant act of injustice, committed by a strong on a weak nation, never before disgraced the annals of history. The attack on Copenhagen has been defended on the plea of necessity ; but the atrocities perpetrated at Badajoz have no such possible excuse. Badajoz was a Spanish fortified town, in possession of the French and was regarded as one of the keys of the Peninsula. Wellington hud been once repulsed from its walls, and on the occasion to which we now refer, it was besieged by him a Sefcond time. After having been intrenched before the place for some days, a practicable breach was made and an assault ordered. As it was known, however, that the French had prepared to defend themselves desperately, it was thought best to stimulate the courage of the storming party bv a distribution of ardent spirits, of which the men were allowed to drink to excess. In this condition they were led to the attack Probably under other circumstances they would have shrunk from the terrible scenes that ensued ; but maddened by what they drank they rushed into the ditch, crossed it, mounted to the

breach, and amid a slaughter unexampled in modern warfare, strove t> force their wav, into the town. The results, when the city was taken, may be guessed. Pillage, con fl igraimn, murder and rape, rioted m the streets and made havoc of French foe and Spanish ally alike. The heart sickens at funding the horrible details ol that sack. And afl this was perpetrated presence in ol a Lli'tish general and by British troops. We might cite other instances in which Gieat Britain has outraged every law. human end divine, in her sanguinary wars. No power, in reality, is more cruel or bloodthirsty, if a shadow of reason eart be shown Why she should be so. We see this in the massacre at Glencoe ; in the hiring Indians to altar k our defenceless frontiers in the Revolution : and in the whole course of her Degressions in the Lust fiom the days of Warren Hastings until now There never has been n people since the Romans, so am- (minus and unprincipled, so þÿ atrocious and þÿbarbarous in their military deeds- Away then with such cant ns that ol the Times I We have had enough of this hypocrisy on the part ot that journal. Whining over Vera Cruz, yet exulting at Badajoz, a pretty specimen of logic and Christianity is tin: London Times! The fact is, the capture of Vein Cruz forms an era in military history ; for never, perhaps, was so strong a post taken with so little loss of life : instead of regretting it, therefore, as does the London Times, we trust the day is not lar distant when military science will render all sieges
as bloodless

Case op Somnambulism. þÿ Altogether the most interesting ease of somnambulism on record is that o( a young ecclesiastic, the narrative of which, from the immediate communication ill an Archbishop of Bordeaux, is given under the head of þÿ þÿSomnambulism friends, in the French I'incyclopa dot. This young ecclesiastic, when the Archbishop was at the same seminary, used to rise every night and write out either sermons or pieces of mude. To study his condition the Archbishop betook himself several nights to the

chamber of the young man, where he made the following observations : þÿ The young man used to rise, to take paper and to write. Before lie wrote music he would take a stick and rule the lines with it. He wrote the notes together with the words corresponding with them with perfect correctness. Or when he had written the words too wide Ire altered them. The notes that were to he black he filled in after he tin il completed the whole. After completing a seiinon he read it aloud Irom beginning to end. If any passage displeased him he erased it and wrote the amended passage correctly over the other. On one occasion he had to substitute the word þÿ to adorable þÿ alter the for þÿ preceding þÿ divin hut he did not omit þÿce into þÿ cel þÿ, by adding the letter þÿ þÿl with exact precision to the word first written. To ascertain whether he used his eyes, the Archbishop interposed a sheet of pasteboard between the writing and his face. He took not the least notice, but went on w riting as before. The limitation of his perceptions to what he was thinking about was vety curious. A bit of aniseed cake that he had sought for, he eat approvingly ; hut when, on another occasion, a piece of the same cake was put in his mouth, he spat it out without observation. The foliowing instance of the dependence of his perceptions upon, or rather their subordination to, his preconceived ideas, is truly wondeitul : þÿ It is to be observed that he always knew when his pen had ink iu it. Likewise, if they adroitly changed his

papers, when he was writing, he knew it. if the sheet substituted was of þÿdifl erentsize from the former, and he appeared embarrassed in that case. But if the fresh sheet of paper, which was substituted for that written on, was exactly of the same size with the former, he appeared not to he aware ol the change. And he would continue to read off his composition from the blank sheet ol paper as fluently as when the manuscript itsell lay before him ; nay, more, he would continue his corrections and introduce the aimnded passage, writing it upon exactly the place on the blank sheet which it would have occupied on the written paper þÿ Blackwood's Magazine.

the supposed injury was forgiven. This tyranny of nflcclion is certainly far fiom agreeable, and the sooner such customs are abolished the better. þÿ Miss Coslellus Wales.

Chateaubrind, in his eloquent work entitled þÿ Genie du Chrisiianisme,' has this beautiful picture of the wife a Christian: þÿ þÿ The wife of a Christian is not a simple mortal; she is a mysteiious, extraordinary, angelic being 1 the flesh of the fl sh, the blood of the blood ol tiie husband. Man, in uniting himself to her, regains a pari ol 1 is sutisiance; hip soul as well us his body are incomplete without his wife; lie has strength, she has beauty ; he combats the enemies of his country and labors in the fields; he does not understand the details ot domos'tc life, hut his companion prepares the repast, and her smiles sweeten existence. tie has crosses, and the partner of his couch is there to soften them : his dais may he sad and troubled, but in the chaste arms of iiis wife he finds comfort and n-pose. þÿ Without woman man would be rude, gross and solitary. How to Sail Against the Wind þÿ The canue was carried down the stream by the lorce of ttie current; but in the afternoon, and during the gieaier part of the night, the sea-breeze blow so strong as to impede our progress. The boatmen, however, adopted a plan to overcome tins, which I have never seen elsewhere, nor ever heard of; and 1 will, therefore, explain it in a few words. þÿ Landing at a place where trees giew in abundance, the men set to work and cut oil a considerable quantity of branches, which were tied tightly together w ith cords ; one end of a long rope was made fast round its middle, while the oilier end was secured to the canoe They then steered for u pail of the river where the current was strong, and threw the bundle overboard ; which, heirg heavy from its green state, floated just below the suifucc of the water, and in tins manner being entirely out of the influence of the wind, it received the whole force of the current ; by which means the canoe was dragged down at a rate little inferior to that by which
we descended during the cn'ti, of the day þÿ Gardner's Travels.

Stores. þÿ A tame stork lived quietly in I lie court yard of the University of Tutbirgen, in Sanbia. till Gmint Victor Gravenits, a student there, shot at a sto þÿk nest s adjacent to the college, and probably wounded the stork in it. This happened in autumn when storks begin their emigrations The next spring a stoi k was observed on the roof of the college, and by its incessant chattering seemed to wish the tame stoik to understand that it would fie glad of its company. But as the wings of the other were dipped, the stranger was induced, with great precaution, to come down first to the upper gallery, the next day something lower, and at last, after much ceremony, quite into ihe court. The tame stork, uncmscious of hairn, went to meet hitn with a cheerful note, when the other fell upon him with the utmost fu'y þÿ The spectators drove away the foreign stoik, but he came again the next day to the charge; and during the whole summer skirmishes were exchanged between them M. Gravenitz had desired that the tame >t-»ik should not be assisted, as, having only a single antagonist, and thus being obliged to shift for himself, he learned to be on his guard, and made such a defence, that at the end of the campaign the stianger hud not much the better of him. Next spring, however, instead of one stork came four, which alighted forthwith in the area, and immediately attacked the tame stoik, who, in t lie view of several persons defended himself with great valour till his strength began to fail, when auxiliaries came

to his assistance All the turkeys, geese, ducks, and fowls that were biought up in the court, probably attached by his mild behaviour, formed a rampart round him, and permitted him a safe retreat. On this a strict r look out was kept against the enemy, till, at the beginning of the third spring, about 20 stoiks alighted in the college and deprived him of fife.

The Moon, so near us, and yel so little known, proves our own incompetency to soar beyond the limits of our eomhined senses- Maps ol the surface 200 years old and liussell's Lunar do be prove tlmi the surface undergoes no change. She can have no (vater on the sine next the Earth. or clouds would obscure her ground plan- She is, in truth, regarded as a dry calx. Her reaction, however, produces a terro-lunar orbit, inversely as the masses, and this orbit scollops the orbit round tfie Sun produced by the fulcrum, or cenite of their momenta. As to the Earth's centre, it is an oscillation to which the mobile oceans respond, and hence the tides. The Egyptians had a tradition that time was when there was no Moon. We are, therefore, to suppose, that in moving through space, in a direction contrary to the Earth, a mutual reaction was established in large and small orbits, like those which constitute the general scheme of the Universe. The dark parts ate not supposed to be water, while the high parts are ridges of mountains or high lauds The brilliant spots are hollows surrounded with high ridges, wttlt a hill in their centre. This rough surface is considered as volcanic; but combustion bespeaks an atmosphere, and observations on the horns prove that there is tine mountain I -3d of a mile high, and another a mile higher. Many Maps have been made of the Moon, and liiciolus and I lovelies assigned names to the several parts, with latitude and longitude taken from lines drawn thiough the

centre. One annular ridge, with a small central rock, just south west of the centre, is called, by one, llipparr-hus, and, by the other, Olympus. A large spot, just south east of the centre, is called Ptolomeus hv one. and Mount Sipylus by the other. 10 43 east and 43" south, is the deep brilliant cavity called Tvclto, or Mount Sinai, the centre of all the radiations in the south. Ily Herschel's observations, we learn that the altitude of the lunar mountains has been much exaggerated. The rock, situated near Locus Sig<-r, is about one mile high ; hut none of the others are more than half. Bailey and others, in observing the annular Eclipse of May, I S36, near the central path, observed such an optical, though peculiar protrusion in the Moon's limb on approaching and leaving the Sun, as led to the conclusion that it must have been produced by an atmosphere. The coldness of the Moon's light is known, but not measured, except hv gardeners. þÿ The heating rays are supposed to be absorbed.

MEXICO. Mexico stands in the centre of a vallcv ; the ancient Mexico, or Tenochtitlan, having been built in the middle of a lake, and connected with the continent by extensive causeways or dikes The new Mexico is three miles Irom the lake of Tezcnco. and nearly six from that of Cha'co; vet Humboldt considers it certain, from the remains of the ancient tcocnlli, or temples, that it occupies the identical position of the former city, and that a great part of the waters of the valley have been dried tip. Mexico was long considered the largest city of America : but it is riots? surpassed by New York, perhaps even by Itio Janeiro, þÿ

Some primates have raised its population to 200,000, hut it may, on go ,u grounds, tie fixed at from 120.000 to 140 000. It is beyond dispute the most splendid of its rivals. The architecture is generally in a very pure style, and there are edifi es of verv beau ifnl structure. The palace of the late vice rovs, the cathedral built in what is termed ihe gothie style, several of the convents arid some private palaces, reared upon plans furnished by the pupils of the Academy of die Fine Arts, are of great extent and magnificence yet, upon the whole, it is rather die arrangement, regularity, and general effect of die city, which render it so admirable, Nothing can lie more enchanting than the view ,d the city and valley from the surrounding heights. The eye sweeps over a vast extent of enhi. vated fields, to the verv base of the colossal mountains covered with perpetual snow. The city appears as if watered by the waters of the lake ol i eecuco. which surrounded hv villages and hamlets, resembles the most beautiful of the Swiss lakes, and the rich cultivation ol the vicinity forms a striking contrast with the naked mountains. Among these rise the famous volcano Popo-Uatepelt, and the mou , tains of Iztaccihualt, of which the first, an enormous cone, burns occasionally, throwing up smoke and ashes in the mtdst of eternal snows. The police of the city is excellent ; most of the streets are handsomely paved, lighted, and cleansed. The markets are remarkably well supplied with animal and vegetable productions,

brought by cro wds of canoes along the lake of Clialeo, and the canal leading to it Most of the flowers and roots have been raised in chinnmpat or floating gardens, an invention peculiar to the New World. They consist of rafts formed of reeds, roots, and bushes, and covered with black saline mould, which, being irrigated by the water of the lake, hecomes exceedingly fertile. The construction of a desague, or canal to carry off the waters of the lake Zumpango. and of the principal river by which it is fed. has prevented any very desolating floods. The desague cost £ I 041)000. and is one of the most stupendous woiks ever executed.

Ottioix or the Marseillaise. þÿ M. de Lnnuiftirie, in his Historic dc Girondint, just published in Paris, gives the following account of the origin of the French national nir, " The Marseillaise " In the garri ,f Strashurg was quartered a young artillery officer, named Kouget de Lisle, a native of Lous le Sauinier, in the Jura He had a great taste for music and poetry, and often entertained his comrades during their long and tedious hours in garrison. Sought after for his musical arid poetical talent, he was a frequent and familiar guest at the house of one Dietrich, an Alsatian patriot, mayor of Strasburg. The winter of 171)2 was a period of great scarcity at Strashurg.. The house of Dietrich was poor, his table was frugal, but n seat was always open to Kouget de Lisle. One day, when there was nothing but bread and some slices of smoked ham on the table, Dietrich, regarding the young officer, said to him with a sad serenity, Abundance fail at our boards, hut what matters that if enthusiasm lails not at our civic files, iior courage in the hearts of our so'diers. I have still a last bottle of wine in my cellar þÿ ' Bring it," said he to one of his dntighteis, " and let us drink to France and liberty. Soasburg should soon have its patiiotic

mtssari r inrr. "' ' i solemnity. Oe Lisle must draw from these last drops one of those hymns which raise the soul of the people" The wine was brought and drunk, after which the officer departed. The night was cold. i>e Lisle was thoughtful. His heart was moved ; Iris head heated. He returned staggering to his solitary room, and slowly sought inspiration, sometimes in the fervour of his citizen soul, and anon ort the keys of instrument, composing now the air before the words and then the words before the air. He sang all and wrote nothing, and at last, exhausted, fell asleep with his head resting on his instrument, and awoke not till day break. The music of the night returned to his mind like the impression of a dream. Ho wrote it, and ran to Dietrich, whom he found in the garden digging winter lectures. The wife and daughters of the old man were not yet up. Dietrich awoke them, and ealied in some friends, alias passionate as himself for music, and able to execute the composition of De Lisle. At the first stanza cheeks grew pale, at the second tears flowed, and at the last the delirium of enthusiasm hurst forth þÿ The wife of Dietrich, his daughters, himself, and the young officer threw themselves cry ing into each other's arms. The hymn of the country was found. Executed some days afterwards in Strasburg the new song flew from city to city, and was played by all the popular orehestras. Marseilles adopted it to be sung at the commencement of the sittings of its clubs, and the Marseillaises spread it through Prance, singing it along the

public roads. Prom this came the name of " Matseillaise." ANECDOTE. We have the following anecdote from an Unquestionable source, and assure our readers that the statement may be relied on þÿ "A gentleman of this city had two cats upon his premises, related by the ties of mother and daughter þÿ both of which weie blessed with a litter of kittens at about the same time. Not many days after, the two mothers were observed siting together in the shed, and intently eyeing each other as ii holding a consultation. Alter the lapse of several minutes thus spent, the younger cat returned to her kitten, the only one having lived, and brought it towards the older cat, which si ill kept tier place. '1 his kitten she placed directly before her mother, and then sat down not far from it The parents looked again at each other for some time, when the older retreated, leaving the kitten where the ottier had placed it. The mother again took up her inewing offspring, and once more approached fier companion, when the same ceremony was repeated with similar effect- This occurred several times, when the older cat, as influenced by the mule appeal of the mother, took the strange kitten thus forced upon her charily, conveyed it to the spot where her darlings were deposited, and to all appearance, adopted it as her own. The younger cat, having seen the object of her solicitude provided for, retired slowly to her straw, where she was soon after taken with a fit and died. We leave it for naturalists to explain whether the invalid cat, was aware of her speedy dissolution or not, or
whether, what we call instinct, in the lower order of animals, does not occasionally approach very near to what is termed reason among the human species." þÿ J\ew JJuven Coin ier.

Delia þÿ Since the arrival of Gen. Taylor, here, all has remained quiet. For for four weeks prior we had at least one stampede in every twenty four hours. All tire troops and everything of value were removed into the Citadel Fori, strong picketguards constantly j«>sted. and tire fort put in a complete state of defence. There seems to he something in lire presence of the Did tlein that inspires every orre si Ir the belief that no harm can come where he is about. With May's squadron of Dragoons and the 1st Mississippi Regiment be has encamped on his old ground nl Walnut Splines. a, [?parent ly in as much security as when Ids whole nrorv was with him. l ire 1st Obi Kcguneut is at the Citadel Fort, and the 1st

Kentucky in the town. The ei'iz- ns me returning to their dwellings, and the maiket, which has been a long time deserted, alloids quite a variety of Mexican edibles. Three days ago the Alcalde and Driest of a small town some 20 miles distant, on oie road to China, came in and reported to Gen. Taylor the murder of 24 Mexicans, at G alopa, a small rancho about six miles from Ramus. The murder was committed, they say, by a party of Americans numberii g about 20, and was done in the night The -murdered men were first made prisoner, tied, and afterward all shot through the head. The murder is said to have been commit, ted on the 28th ult. On tlist night a train of loaded waggons, escorted by 2(10 uiiuniry and about the same number of horses, una- r command of Col. Mitchell, of the 1st Ohio Regiment, encamped at Mann, which is about five miles from the scene of the minder. The mounted men were composed of U S. Dragoons and Texas Rangeis, under u,e Command of Capt. Graham, of the 2 i Diu goons. Suspicion ress upon some put of this corps, though no clue has as yet b'Ui found to discover the guilty. The officers in command þÿ gentlemen and rigid disciplinarians þÿ are using eveiy means in their power to investigate the matter þÿ Gen Taylor hag got his steam up <m the subject, and is determined to have hung eve ry one who it cau be proved, has taken pint in the murder. The town where these men were killed is but a few nuies from the place where the large train was captured and so many waggoners massacred on the 22d of

February Some 15 or 20 of the waggoners who escaped front that massacre came up in the last train, yet there is no evidence that they were engaged in the Guulopa minder. 1 passed over the place of the massacre of the 22d February a few days ago, and the scene is truly the most horrid and revolting that 1 have ever witnessed. The remains of the murdered men, vet unburied, stripped of every particle ot clothing, lay upon the plains, their flush devoured by Mexican wolves and bussards, and their bones bleaching in the sun. The train was a very large and valuable one, and stretched out from three to tour miles in length. The attack was made upon the escort, þÿ who were in the advance, by a large body of Lancers. The escort, 40 men, under Lieut, Barbour, of the Kentucky Legion, weie all taken ptisotiers. and are now in the possession of Urrea. The Lancers charged down the trail), and lanced without mercy the waggoners, as they ran for their lives to the chapporal. More than three four ths of them, it is thought, were killed, and their bodies shockingly mutilated and disfigured. Those who passed the scene a few dat a after, say that sooie had their heuits cut out and suspended upon the hushes, or thrust into theifimoutlis ; tire eyes of others were dug from their 6ockeis, and inserted in wound made in other parts of their bodies ; and other mutilations were performed thai would make even a JNoith American savage blush to look at. Yet these acts were committed bv Gen, Urrea's men þÿ the regular

soldiers of the Mexican army ! Urrea, by last accounts, was at Linares, expecting re-infotoemenis. It is nmi< n d that he has four pieces of at nllery with i.uu. Marin, GerrnKo, Mier and Cliinn will all soon be gatrisoned by out ttoops, which will

render our communication with Camttrgo entirely safe. The troops here are hi excel lent health and condition. The Kentucky Legion leave on Monday for 'Jamargo, as an escort to a train. These troops have hut six weeks to serve, and as it is Gen Taylor's intention. I hear, to discharge them at New Oileans. 1 presume they Will not return again. The Ohio troops have about eight weeks to serve þÿ their turn w ill probably come next. The number of regiments whose year will expire in May or June, now in Gen. Taylor's column, is iliir t6en. How their places are to be filled I cannot devise þÿ perhaps you eon infoim us. We are looking with great anxiety for tiews fmm Gen. Scott. Nothing of inten si from Salttllo or Agua Nueva. The surgeot.s report our wounded doing remarkably well Of the whole number wounded in the 1st Mississippi Regiment, only one amputate n was required. The wounds, generally, are from musket balls, and of course slight com pared to those made by Cannon, grape and canister at the battle fought here. The position of our troops at the battle of Boena Vista rendered the artillery of the enemy almost entirely ineffectual: not more than eight of otir men were injured by cannon shot, Should anything of interest occur I will write you by the next train. DISTRESS IX MADURA, We are indebted to Mr. Burden, an inteliigent gentleman from Madeira, at present in this City, for some information relating to the famine which has vexed and is vexing that Island. He says, that for months past, the poor inhabitants of Madeira have been in as deplorable a condition as the suffering Irish. The Potato crop has failed for two years ; nnd this calamity, followed hy a deficiency in the supply of Breadstuff's þÿ in consequence of the rise of pi ices in this and other countries þÿ has left the poor there without any of the most absolute necessaries of life to depend upon. The mother country, Portugal, could not aid them, if it would. Immersed in all the evils of rebellion, nnd insurrectionary tints, the Government of that country can hardly maintain itself; probably will be compelled to call in foreign assistance. The Government of the Island has done all in its power for the needy and destitute; but all was necessarily little: for (lie Government itself is poor. Our ships, speeding across the Ocean upon their errand of ntercy to the suffering in Ireland. might leave a part of their charitable f eight at Madeira, or vessels could be fitted out for the exclusive purpose The Portuguese. equally with the Irish, are our allies ; a id suffering makes them equally our btethren. The high prices of all kinds of Breadstuff's in the Island would justify the sending there of a few vessels, loaded with Grain, on specul ition ; and persons who cannot aff'oid to
make gratuitous contributions, might realize n handsome and hy no means censurable profit from the assistance thus þÿrendered. Ib.

The following imporiant ukase has just been received from St Petersburg!), and has caused great excitement in i he moneyed circles of the metropolis, as it is generally believed that a large proportion of the immense sum named will be invested in the English funds : þÿ " By command of his Imperial Majesty, the Directing Situate heatd the icport ol the AJ iiiist.tr ol Finance of the 1st of April, under No. gi!3.» in which he presents for due publication a milium confirmed by his Imperial Majesty of the 31st of March last, containing the opinion of the Council of the Empire to the follow ing cilect : þÿ 1 he Council of the Empire in the department of economy and in general assembly, having examined the statement of tltc Minister of Finance relative to the laving aside, out of ihe bullion capital of tile department of credit billets, of a sum of 30,000 000 of silver rubles for ihe purchase of public securities, and acknowledging for its own part the utility of this step, because it appears a convenient and promising means of extracting out of the immense bullion fund (mote than 1 14 000 000 id silver rubles, or nearl.ti 20 000 000/ sterling), hitherto dormaid, important advantages lor the empire, foresees no obstacle to ihe adoption of it, on this sole condition þÿ that the said advantages must he applied exclusively to the extinction of the various debts of the empire. From this point of view, this measure offers I he following results: þÿ " 1. That the bullion capital, in its ftx'M

amount, is in no respect diminished, but only a portion of the coin hi it replaced by seenri ties equally solid and valuable, and which moreover bring in a constant income, and enjoy universal credit through Europe. ' 2 The quantity of coin of our bullion capital, altei setting aside the part appreciated to the put chase of securities, is still so enormous, that, judging by our experience, and that of foreign banks, it cannot but be deemed sufficient for the uninterrupted conversion of the billets de cieilit; but even should a necessity arise for the increase of the quantity of coin in the bullion fund, then the aforesaid securities oiler thereto every convenience, by the ready sale of the same for cash. " 3. The use of the advantage which may accrue from such an operation, being exclusively applicable to the extinction ol the debts of the empire, promises to the gover nincut new means for the satisfaction of its engagements, and consequently a corresponding alleviation of the national burdens. Considering these things, the Council of the Empire has given its opinion as follows: þÿ 1. ' From the separate capital lixod by the 3 tli and 17th paragraphs of the Imperial manifesto ol the 1st ol June, 1813, for the conversion ot the billets de credit into cash, a sum should beset npaii to the extent of 30 000,000 of silver rubles for the gradual purchase of public securities, llussiati and foreign, here and abroad. "2. These securities, as they are bought, arc In be reckoned as belonging to the said
capital at the value paid tor them, and are to be preserved together with ihe ready uiouey.

3 The interest or rentes ol tli se Inn. is. accruing from these securities, and, in hue, all the profits of the opetalion, should lo devoted to the extinction of the foreign and interminable debts of the empire; but, in the event of the purchased securities falling 2 or 3 per cent., below the price at which tbey were purchased, a portion ol the said dividends or rentes is lo be reckoned to the account of the bullion capital, till it equals the monev laid out, using for the extinction of the debts ol the etnpiie only the residue. Since the diligencia went out at noon today for Vera Cruz, another diligencia has come in from the city of Mexico full of passengers and bringing news of not a little of importance. Among the passengers was Mr. Kennedy, who, after being badly treated here about the 1st of Apnl was driven to the city of Mexico. All the passengers confirm what 1 wrote you this morning. They say that at the capital there was no Government, no order, no responsibility all þÿ was anaichy. Anaya was still President pro tern, but had neilher influence nor authority. A new President is to be elected on the 15th of the present month þÿ the tenth chief magistrate this distracted country has had within the last eighteen months. The ladrones þÿ guerrillas, I suppose they should he called now þÿ are busy at work upon the roads, especially between Puebla and the city of Mexico. It is stated that the propositions made by England some mouths since, to oiler her intervention in settling t lie difficulties between Mexico and the United States, have recently been taken up by the Mexican Congress, and

after a warm discussion, in which one of the members said that the whole affair was but another attempt of the monarchists upon the sacred liberties of the Mexican Republic, the motion even to consider them was lost by a vote of 44 to 33. Santa Anna, so far as I can learn, is the only man who has been spoken of in Mexico as a candidate for the Presidency, and lie is in very bad order wiih the mass. The states north of þÿMexico Guadalajara, Guanajuato, Queretaro, Zacatecas. Durango, San Luis and others þÿ talk openly of separating from Mexico, and letting her take care of herself. Not a dollar in the wav of supplies are they sending on for the relief of the General Government in its emergency. They were still doing a lit tie in the way of fortifying the city of Mexico, hut a Spaniard informs me that all the obstructions they have erected so far could be kicked over with the foot. The city had been placed under martini law, and the direst excesses were anticipated. The citizens had all been colled upon to take up arms in t he common defence but unfortunately nine tenths of them had no arms to take up. Nor were there any cannon at the capital other than a few small and indifferent pieces. There is certainly a party, and an influential one, in Mexico, which begins to talk of peace; and where four weeks since they did not dare breathe their sentiments, they now come out openly and avow themselves Still the measure is far from popular. The peace party is composed ol the more
honest and intelligent property holders, the merchants and perhaps the clergy þÿ to these are opposed the military who have ail dis graced themselves, and all the demagogues

among the lawyers If the priests could be made certain that they would continue to hold their rich benefices secure, they would probably be all in favor of peace. On approach of the Americans it is said that Congress, with all the archives ol the Republic, will move to the city of Moielia. Majors Borland and Games, Capt G. M. Just as my express man was starting, 1 was fortunate enough to get hold of the following hurried translation of a proclamation, which has been printed in Spanish, and addressed by Gen- Scott to the Mexicans. I have no lime to peruse it, hut those who have think it will have weight and influence with the Mexicans. In haste, K. The following is the proclamation mentioned by Mr. Kendall. In justice to General Scott, it must he borne in mind that the original has undergone two þÿtranslations first into the Spanish and then back into English, j Headquarters of the Army, i Jalapa, May, II, ) The General-in-Chief of the Armies of the United Stales of America to the Mexican Nation ; Mexicans ! The recent events of the war, and the measures adopted in consequence by

your Government, make it my duty to address you þÿ to show you truths of which you arc ignorant, because they have been criminally concealed fiom you. 1 do not ask you to trust my words, (though he who has never falsified them has a light to confidence) hut to judge of these truths by facts within the view and knowledge of you all. Whatever may have been the origin of this war, which my country saw itself forced to undertake by irremediable causes, which I learn are unknown to the greater part of the Mexican nation, we regard it as a necessity ; such is it always to both belligerents, and reason and justice, if not forgotten on both sides, are in dispute, each believing them its own. You have proof of this truth as wpII as ourselves, for in Mexico, as in the United States, there have existed and do exist two opposite parties desiring þÿ the one peace, the other war. But Governments have sacred duties, from which they cannot depart ; and often these duties impose, for national reasons, n silence and a reserve sometimes displeasing to the majority of those who, from views puiely personal or individual, make opposition. We have seen and þÿ we cannot be taxed with partiality for þÿlamenting with astonishment that the heroic deportment of the gar i i son of Vera Cruz, in its valiant defence, was aspersed by the general who had just been defeated and put to shameful (light by a force far inferior to that which he commanded at Buena Vista; that this general, rewarding the insurgents and promoters of civil war in Mexico, heaped outrage on those who had singularly distinguished themselves by a resistance beyond what could be expected, and of admirable decision Finally, the bloody event of Uerro Gordo fins shown the Mexican nation what it may reasonably expect if it longer continues blind to the true situation in which it has been placed bv some generals, whom it has most distinguished and m whom it has most confided. From the Houston Telegraph , May 10. Mexican Tuadbhs. þÿ A. large paity of Mexican traders arrived al Bexar on the 22d ult., from the vicinity of Santa Rosa. They brought" a large number ol horses, mules, pclouces Az<: , which they intended to ex change foi goods. These traders report that the Texan volunteers in the Rio Grande valley have been authorized by Gen. Taylor lo punish all the alcaldes and large hacienda holders who turned against the Americans while Urrea was in that section. They des troyed several large rai dies and drove oil the rancheros and peons who were engaged with the Mexican guerilla parties. This has spread such a panic among the Mexicans that the alcaldes, priests, and other leading m n, no longer dare to overawe the people or attempt to prevent them tiom trading with the Americans. Fitleen or twenty alcaldes have been thrown into prison, and many others have lied into the interior, fearing that they will be executed lor the murdeis that have been committed at the towns where they resided It appears, from the representations ol ihe tradeis, that the Mexicans in the llio Grande valley have become completely humbled, and evince the most perfect submission to the Americans. It is believed that thousands of them will soon flock to Bexar and other towns on our western Irontiers to liade with our citizens. They no longer refuse lo sell their horses or mules, hut are w illing to trade any article they possess, as freely as previous to (tie revolution. The guerilla hands seem to have en-

tirely disappeared since our volunteers have commenced scouring the country. We no longer hear of Canales, Carabajal, Falcon, or any other guerilla chiols ; they have either reiired into the interior, or have concealed themselves in some ol the mountain lecesses; nor is it probable that they will again venture to commit depredations while the volunteers remain in that section.

A þÿParrot s Memory. þÿ The following well authenticated anecdote has something human about it. A parrot had been caught young, and trained by a Spanish lady, who sold it to an English sea captain. For a time the bird seemed sad among the togs of England, where birds and men all spoke to her in a foreign tongue. By degrees, however, site learned the language, forgot her Spanish phrases, and seemed to feel at home. Years passed on, and found pretty Foil the pet of the captain's family. At last her brilliant feathers began to turn grey with age: sha could take no food but soft pulp, and had not strength to mount her perch. But none had the heart to kill the old favourite, she was entwined with so many pleasant household recollections She had been some time in this feeble condition, when a Spanish gentleman called one day to see her master. It was the fust time she had heard the language for many years. It brought hack to memory ihe scenes of her youth in that beautiful region of vines and sunshine. Site spread forth her wings with a wild scream of joy, rapidly ran over the Spanish phrases, winch she had not uttered for years, and fell down dead. þÿ Letters from New York , by Maiia Child

For What is a Mother Responsible. A Mother is usually also a wife, and has the management ot a family and a direct influence over those within her appropriate sphere. She owes subordination of couise,

to Iter head, but site has the seat of authority and wields the government. Fretii a position of entire dependence she has lisen ro power and rank 5 arid though hot throne be in a cottage and her dominion the little world of household aflaits, yet she is not the less really responsible than is that youthful Queen who now sways a sceptre over a large portion of the four quarters of the earth. But for what is she responsible? She is responsible for the rearing and nursing of her progeny s for their physical constitution and growths their exercise and proper sustenance through early life, A child left to grow up deformed, bloated, or tneagre, is an object of maternal negligence. She is responsible for their deportment. þÿ She can make them fearful or cringing ; she can make ti.cm modest or impertinent ; ingenuous or deceitful ; me.iu or inanlv ; clownish or polite. The germ of ail these things is in childhood, and a mother can repress or firing them forth. She is responsible for the principles indulealed in early life. For her ilis to say whether those who go forth from her fireside shall be imbued with sentiments of vinue, truth, honour, honesty, temperance, industry, benevolence, or those of a 'contrary character þÿ vice, ftaud, drunkenness, idleness, covetousness. There ast will be found to be of the most natural growth, but on her is devolved the daily, hourly task of weeding her little garden þÿ of eradicating those odious productions, and planting the human heart with the lillv, and

the rose, and the amaranth, that fadeless flower, emblem of truth. 8ho is to a very cum-iderable extent responsitde for the temper and disposition of her children. Constitutionally they may he violent iriitable, or revengeful ; but for the regulation or correction of these passions a mother is responsible. Siie is responsible for the intellectual acquire-merits ol Iter children, she is bound to do what she can for this object. Schools, academies, and colleges, open their portals throughout the land ; and every mother is under heavy responsibilities to see that her sons and daughters have ail the benefits which these afford, and which their circumstances will permit thorn to enjoy. She is responsible for dieir religious education The beginning of all wisdom is the fear of God ; and this every mother must teach. Reverence for God, acquaintance with his word, respect for the du'ics and ordinance of religion, are within the ability of every parent to implant : and if her Children should grow up ignorant or regardless of the Bible and their Saviour, what mother, when she considers the wickedness of the human heart, can expect them to rise up and calf her blessed ?
